info.name: S2 Components Demo
info.description:
Module S2: Core Spring AI components demonstration

## Learning Objectives
- Master ChatClient vs ChatModel usage patterns
- Understand prompt templating and system messages
- Learn structured output and entity mapping
- Explore streaming responses and metadata access
- Compare high-level vs low-level API approaches

## Why This Module Exists
This module provides comprehensive examples of Spring AI's core components. It demonstrates the practical differences between ChatClient and ChatModel, teaching when to use each approach and how to leverage advanced features like streaming, templates, and structured outputs.

## Key Learning Concepts
- **API Abstraction Levels**: Understanding when to use high-level vs low-level APIs
- **Prompt Engineering**: System messages, templates, and structured prompts
- **Response Processing**: Metadata extraction, streaming, and type-safe outputs
- **Performance Patterns**: Streaming for better user experience

## Testing Prerequisites
- Application running: `./mvnw spring-boot:run`
- Valid OpenAI API key configured
- Understanding of JSON structure for requests

item.name: ChatClient Demonstrations

request.description:
Demonstrates basic ChatClient usage with fluent API.

**Why ChatClient is preferred:**
- **Fluent API**: More readable and intuitive
- **Built-in best practices**: Handles common patterns automatically
- **Type safety**: Better compile-time checking
- **Extensibility**: Easy to add advisors and customizations

**Trade-offs:**
- **Abstraction**: Less direct control over OpenAI API
- **Learning curve**: New API to learn vs familiar ChatModel
- **Flexibility**: May not cover every edge case

**When to use ChatClient:**
- Standard chat applications (90% of use cases)
- Rapid prototyping and development
- When you want Spring AI best practices built-in
- Future-proof applications (ChatClient is the strategic direction)

request.description:
Demonstrates system message usage for AI personality control.

**Why system messages are crucial:**
- **Behavior control**: Define AI personality and response style
- **Context setting**: Establish role and expertise domain
- **Consistency**: Maintain character across conversation
- **Safety**: Set behavioral boundaries and guidelines

**System message best practices:**
- Be specific and clear about expected behavior
- Include handling instructions for edge cases
- Set boundaries for what the AI should/shouldn't do
- Define the expertise level and tone

**Trade-offs:**
- **Token usage**: System messages consume tokens
- **Rigidity**: May limit AI's natural responses
- **Complexity**: Crafting good system messages requires skill

**Common pitfalls:**
- Overly complex system messages
- Conflicting instructions
- Not testing edge cases

request.description:
Demonstrates prompt templating for structured content generation.

**Why use prompt templates:**
- **Consistency**: Standardized prompt structure
- **Reusability**: Same template, different parameters
- **Maintainability**: Centralized prompt management
- **Quality**: Tested and optimized prompts

**Template design principles:**
- Clear parameter placeholders
- Flexible but structured format
- Include examples and constraints
- Consider output format requirements

**Trade-offs:**
- **Flexibility vs Structure**: Templates may limit creativity
- **Complexity**: Template syntax adds learning curve
- **Maintenance**: Templates need updates and testing

**Alternatives considered:**
- String concatenation (rejected: error-prone, hard to maintain)
- Dynamic prompt building (rejected: complex, inconsistent)
- External template engines (rejected: unnecessary complexity)

**Common pitfalls:**
- Over-complex templates with too many parameters
- Not validating parameter values
- Templates that are too rigid or too loose

request.description:
Demonstrates accessing response metadata for monitoring and analytics.

**Why metadata is important:**
- **Cost tracking**: Monitor token usage and API costs
- **Performance monitoring**: Track response times and quality
- **Analytics**: Understand usage patterns
- **Debugging**: Investigate issues and optimize prompts

**Key metadata fields:**
- **Usage statistics**: Prompt tokens, completion tokens, total tokens
- **Model information**: Which model was used
- **Timing data**: Processing duration
- **Quality indicators**: Confidence scores, safety flags

**Production applications:**
- Cost optimization through token monitoring
- Performance dashboards and alerting
- A/B testing different prompts or models
- Compliance and audit trails

**Trade-offs:**
- **Storage overhead**: Metadata requires additional storage
- **Processing cost**: Extracting metadata takes time
- **Complexity**: More data to manage and analyze

**Best practices:**
- Log metadata for production monitoring
- Set up alerts for unusual token usage
- Use metadata for prompt optimization
- Include metadata in debugging workflows

request.description:
Demonstrates Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming for real-time responses.

**Why streaming is crucial for chat applications:**
- **User experience**: Immediate feedback, no waiting for complete response
- **Perceived performance**: Users see progress, feel more engaged
- **Large responses**: Better handling of long-form content
- **Real-time feel**: Mimics human conversation patterns

**Implementation details:**
- Uses Server-Sent Events (SSE) protocol
- Content-Type: text/event-stream
- Flux<ChatResponse> for reactive streams
- Client receives chunks as they're generated

**Trade-offs:**
- **Complexity**: More complex than simple request/response
- **Connection management**: Need to handle stream lifecycle
- **Error handling**: Partial responses on failures
- **Caching**: Streaming responses can't be easily cached

**Alternatives considered:**
- WebSockets (rejected: overkill for one-way streaming)
- Polling (rejected: inefficient, poor user experience)
- Long polling (rejected: complex, doesn't solve the UX problem)

**Best practices:**
- Always include proper error handling
- Set reasonable timeouts
- Handle client disconnection gracefully
- Consider fallback to non-streaming for compatibility

request.description:
Demonstrates structured output with automatic entity mapping to Java objects.

**Why structured output is revolutionary:**
- **Type safety**: Compile-time checking of response structure
- **No parsing**: Direct mapping to Java objects
- **Validation**: Built-in data validation
- **Integration**: Seamless integration with Java applications

**How it works:**
- AI generates JSON conforming to Java class structure
- Spring AI automatically deserializes to POJOs
- Bean Validation annotations ensure data quality
- Records provide immutable, clean data structures

**Advantages over string parsing:**
- **Reliability**: No parsing errors or malformed data
- **Maintainability**: Changes to structure are compile-time safe
- **Performance**: No manual JSON parsing overhead
- **Documentation**: Class structure serves as API documentation

**Trade-offs:**
- **Rigidity**: Response must conform to predefined structure
- **AI understanding**: AI must understand and follow schema
- **Complexity**: More complex than simple string responses
- **Debugging**: Harder to debug when AI doesn't follow schema

**Best practices:**
- Use clear, descriptive field names
- Include validation annotations
- Provide examples in prompts
- Handle parsing failures gracefully
- Use records for immutable data structures

**Common pitfalls:**
- Overly complex nested structures
- Ambiguous field names or types
- Not providing clear examples to the AI
- Missing validation and error handling

item.name: ChatModel Demonstrations

request.description:
Demonstrates basic ChatModel usage - the lower-level Spring AI API.

**When to use ChatModel over ChatClient:**
- **Fine-grained control**: Need direct access to OpenAI API features
- **Custom response processing**: Complex response handling requirements
- **Legacy integration**: Working with existing ChatModel-based code
- **Performance optimization**: Minimal overhead requirements

**ChatModel characteristics:**
- **Direct API access**: Closer to OpenAI's native API
- **Manual message handling**: You manage message structure
- **Lower abstraction**: More code but more control
- **Explicit configuration**: All settings must be specified

**Trade-offs vs ChatClient:**
- **Pros**: More control, closer to OpenAI API, potentially faster
- **Cons**: More boilerplate, manual best practices, harder to maintain

**Migration path:**
- ChatModel is not deprecated, both APIs will coexist
- New projects should generally prefer ChatClient
- Existing ChatModel code can remain unchanged
- Consider ChatClient for new features even in ChatModel projects

request.description:
Demonstrates structured prompt building with multiple message types using ChatModel.

**Multiple message types in ChatModel:**
- **System messages**: Set AI behavior and expertise
- **User messages**: The actual user input/query
- **Assistant messages**: Previous AI responses (for conversation history)
- **Context messages**: Additional background information

**Why structured prompts matter:**
- **Role clarity**: Each message type has a specific purpose
- **Context control**: Fine-grained control over what information is included
- **Conversation flow**: Proper message sequencing for multi-turn conversations
- **Token optimization**: Include only necessary context

**ChatModel advantages for complex prompts:**
- **Message array control**: Direct manipulation of message sequence
- **Role specification**: Explicit control over message roles
- **Custom message types**: Can include metadata and custom fields
- **Debugging**: Easier to inspect exact messages sent to API

**Best practices:**
- Keep system messages focused and clear
- Use appropriate message roles (system/user/assistant)
- Include relevant context without overwhelming the prompt
- Test different message orderings for optimal results

**Common patterns:**
- System message → Context → User message
- System message → Conversation history → User message
- Multiple context messages → User query

request.description:
Demonstrates ChatModel with custom OpenAI configuration options.

**ChatModel configuration advantages:**
- **Direct option control**: Explicit parameter specification
- **Per-request configuration**: Different settings for different requests
- **Option validation**: Clear understanding of what options are available
- **Cost control**: Precise token and model management

**Key configuration options:**
- **temperature** (0.0-2.0): Controls response creativity/randomness
- **maxTokens**: Maximum response length (cost control)
- **model**: Specific OpenAI model selection
- **topP**: Alternative to temperature for nucleus sampling
- **presencePenalty**: Reduces repetition
- **frequencyPenalty**: Reduces common phrases

**Temperature guidelines:**
- **0.0-0.3**: Factual, consistent, deterministic responses
- **0.4-0.7**: Balanced creativity and accuracy (default range)
- **0.8-1.0**: Creative, varied, more unpredictable responses
- **1.1-2.0**: Highly creative, potentially inconsistent

**Model selection strategy:**
- **gpt-4**: Highest quality, most expensive, slower
- **gpt-4-turbo**: Good balance of quality and speed
- **gpt-3.5-turbo**: Fastest, cheapest, good for simple tasks

**Cost optimization patterns:**
- Use appropriate model for task complexity
- Set reasonable maxTokens limits
- Monitor token usage via metadata
- Cache responses when possible

request.description:
Demonstrates multi-turn conversation handling within a single ChatModel request.

**Single-request conversation pattern:**
- **Complete history**: Send entire conversation in one request
- **Context preservation**: All previous messages included
- **Stateless service**: No server-side session management
- **Full control**: Manual message history management

**Why this pattern is useful:**
- **Simplicity**: No session management complexity
- **Scalability**: Stateless services scale better
- **Debugging**: Full conversation visible in single request
- **Flexibility**: Client controls conversation flow

**Message roles in conversation:**
- **system**: Sets AI behavior and personality
- **user**: Human inputs and questions
- **assistant**: AI responses and explanations

**Trade-offs vs session-based conversations:**
- **Pros**: Stateless, scalable, simple debugging
- **Cons**: Repeated data transfer, client complexity, token usage

**Best practices:**
- Include full conversation context for coherent responses
- Use appropriate system messages for consistency
- Manage conversation length to avoid token limits
- Consider conversation summarization for very long histories

**When to use this pattern:**
- Stateless architectures
- Simple conversation flows
- When you need full control over conversation history
- API-only services without session management

request.description:
Demonstrates streaming responses with ChatModel for real-time content delivery.

**ChatModel streaming implementation:**
- **Direct stream control**: Lower-level access to streaming mechanics
- **Manual chunk handling**: You control how chunks are processed
- **Custom SSE formatting**: Can customize Server-Sent Events structure
- **Error handling**: Direct control over stream error scenarios

**Streaming with ChatModel vs ChatClient:**
- **ChatModel**: More control, manual implementation, custom formats
- **ChatClient**: Built-in best practices, standardized format, easier implementation

**Implementation considerations:**
- **Backpressure handling**: Managing client consumption rate
- **Connection management**: Handling client disconnections
- **Error propagation**: How to handle mid-stream errors
- **Completion signaling**: Indicating end of stream

**Performance characteristics:**
- **Lower latency**: First token appears quickly
- **Better UX**: Users see progress immediately
- **Resource usage**: Streams require persistent connections
- **Caching complexity**: Streaming responses are harder to cache

**Production considerations:**
- Connection pooling for streaming endpoints
- Timeout management for long-running streams
- Load balancer configuration for persistent connections
- Monitoring stream health and completion rates

**When to choose ChatModel streaming:**
- Need custom stream format or processing
- Integrating with existing streaming infrastructure
- Require fine-grained control over streaming behavior
- Building specialized streaming applications
